title: Half-marathon running performance is not improved by a rate of fluid intake above that dictated by thirst sensation in trained distance runners
authors: Dion T, Savoie FA, Asselin A, Gariepy C, Goulet ED
population: 10 trained distance runners in two randomised 21.1-km treadmill time trials at 30 C and 42% relative humidity
findings: Programmed fluid intake (about 1,380 mL/h, to keep body mass loss under 2%) reduced dehydration from 3.1 to 1.3% body weight, rectal temperature from 39.4 to 39.1 C and heart rate from 175 to 171 bpm compared with thirst-driven drinking (about 384 mL/h).
Half-marathon time did not differ between trials (thirst-driven 89.8 +/- 7.7 min, programmed 89.6 +/- 7.7 min), nor did pace.
The authors conclude that programmed fluid intake offers no performance benefit over thirst-driven drinking during a half marathon in warm conditions.
limitations: Ten trained runners (about 90 min), on a treadmill; water only, so the study says nothing about carbohydrate drinks; a 1,380 mL/h programme is far above what a recreational road runner would drink.
implications: In a warm half marathon at about 90 min, drinking to thirst (about 3% body-mass loss) was as fast as drinking about 1.4 L/h. Supports 'drink to thirst' wording for the half and does not support forcing fluid.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (EJAP 113:3011-3020). Abstract read on Europe PMC and PubMed (PubMed used for the '<2%' symbols). Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
